content:
Faced with a surge in reports of "AI slop" vulnerabilities, Apple has recently adjusted its bug bounty programme. Details below.

Apple limits unprocessed bug reports

Apple confirmed to the Financial Times that it has "set a cap and a 30-day cooling-off period for submissions to its internal vulnerability portal, requiring users to request a higher quota."

The measures, implemented in June, are intended to address a wider industry surge in vulnerability reports. As large language models become increasingly powerful — able to discover, string together and exploit vulnerabilities — review teams are struggling to keep up with submissions.

Several weeks ago, Apple had already confirmed that, in response to these AI tools, it was accelerating security updates, front-running patches in iOS 26.5.2 and its counterparts that had originally been planned for last week's 26.6 release.

In the security notes for all these systems, Apple acknowledged researchers who used AI tools from companies including OpenAI, Anthropic and Z.ai, thanking them for helping uncover multiple vulnerabilities.

One of the teams acknowledged was Calif.io, which said in May that, using Anthropic's Mythos Preview model, it had built a working macOS kernel memory corruption exploit on an M5 chip in just five days.

Days before the Financial Times report was published, GitHub introduced a tiered system in its own bug bounty programme, aimed at curbing AI slop while differentiating submissions from experienced security researchers.

The Financial Times report tells the story of Bynario — a seven-person cybersecurity startup that has in recent years used AI tools and models to find vulnerabilities, submitting five reports to Apple this year and eight from last year, "one of which was patched in a November software update," only to have its submissions blocked.

Following the Financial Times report, Apple has reached out to Bynario and is reviewing its findings, including a privilege escalation exploit chain that could give attackers full control of a Mac.

Apple's statement on the recent bug bounty changes, issued to the Financial Times:

The company added that researchers "can easily request a higher limit at any time to ensure that significant reports reach our security team."
